doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Defining groove and music for dancing
summary: Johnson defines groove as everything moving together, and recalls Joe Williams saying music was for dancing, and avant-garde losing the audience.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I’ve got a definition I want to ask you about. Because this is kind of elusive, but you just give us your own words. You know playing rhythm guitar, setting up sometimes counter rhythms. If the bass is walking quarter notes, and sometimes you have to drop chords and spaces all around without, without, sometimes without doing the Freddie Green thing on every beat. But can you give us your definition of what you would call groove. What is groove?

It’s called a lot of things. It’s called groove, it’s called pocket, it’s called just like right on it. But I think groove is the feel when everything moves right together. It’s like the bass player is the water, the piano player is the part of the boat, and the guitar player is like deck one, and the singer is at the helm. And all of you are just sailing and you’re on the © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

groove. Everybody just sails right along and you can feel it. There’s another thing that I got from Joe, and singers in general, but he told me that, you know, when he was coming up that music was for dancing. And we sort of got away from that. And when calls off a tempo, and a lot of guys, when they get ready to call off a tempo of a song, they’re always thinking about where you would dance to it. And every time, without fail, for the last 28 years that I have seen the old guys call off the tempo of a song, people immediately start moving their bodies right away. Because those guys knew that the music was for dancing. And there is a certain rhythm or a certain tempo that the body just moves with, you know. It’s not jerky or anything like that, it just grooves right along and Joe has it. I mean he does it all of the time. And I notice this all the time, because he was right, music is for dancing, you know, when they were coming up. But I think that we got real, when the avante garde stuff came and stuff like that it lost the audience. Because they couldn’t relate to it, and they couldn’t feel it either, you know? I think that you can probably get away with a lot of stuff if you just swing like mad. But when you don’t have that, and you’re not swinging either, it loses people.
Didn’t Ellington say something about that?
That’s right. If it don’t have that swing, you know, what’s it about.
